newsitem.title: MACAU: Big turnout in Macau's last poll before China rule.
newsitem.headline: Big turnout in Macau's last poll before China rule.

text.p: Voters in Macau flocked to cast their ballots on Sunday in the territory's last legislative elections under Portuguese rule, before it reverts to China in 1999.

A big turnout of voters braved intermittent squalls to have their say -- the narrow, cobbled inner city now quiet in the aftermath of a cacophony of loudhailers, patriotic songs and campaign karaoke that had accompanied the final flurry of electioneering.
"I'm very happy these are the last elections under Portuguese rule," said retired merchant Pedro Cheong. "To me, Macau is already part of China."
By mid-afternoon about 35 percent of the more than 100,000 registered voters had cast their ballots, almost four times the total turnout of the last legislative elections in 1992.
"It is our duty to vote because the new legislature will go beyond 1999 when Macau returns to China," said 28-year-old clerk Maria Cheang, who voted for a pro-democracy candidate.
Only eight of the Legislative Assembly's 23 seats are being directly contested in Sunday's poll.
The remainder of the assembly, which will straddle the handover to China on December 20, 1999, are either indirectly elected or appointed by the governor.

Ruled by Portugal for almost five centuries, and like nearby Hong Kong, this tiny territory of 424,000 mainly ethnic Chinese is set to become an autonomous Special Administrative Region of China under Beijing's plan to reunify lost territories.
But while the enclave, a rocky outcrop nestled at the southern tip of China, seems to lack campaign issues, it has never lacked scandal.
Best known for its casinos, the territory has regularly hit the headlines for vice, violence and a wave of gangland bombings.
More recently, the 14-day election campaign has been dogged by rumours of bribery and vote-rigging, with several complaints already due to be investigated.
Local newspapers have reported that some groups had spent up to large sums to buy votes, with residents paid up to 2,500 patacas (US$320) to register to vote.

Some affluent candidates organised limousine and bus shuttle services free-of-charge for voters, while others had hundreds of their supporters on the streets to "assist" electors in finding the polling booths.

Macau's electoral system is only partly democratic. Voters directly elect eight members of the assembly, while eight are indirectly elected by business, labour and community organisations, and seven are appointed by the governor.
A record 62 candidates are vying for the eight directly elected seats.
In contrast to the British colony of Hong Kong, which reverts to China next July 1, Macau's assembly is not fighting for its survival beyond the 1999 handover,
Beijing has given Macau's election process a nod of approval, not only allowing it to straddle the handover but extending its four-year tenure to 2001.
Voting was set to end at 8 p.m. (1200 GMT) with a result expected in the early hours of Monday.
